headline: Oktoberfest Operator Hands Out Free Shorts to Protect Women
meta_description: An 80-year-old amusement ride operator at Munich's Oktoberfest has distributed over 100 pairs of free cycling shorts to women, protecting them from voyeuristic…
summary_short: At Munich's Oktoberfest, the operator of the Teufelsrad has given away more than 100 pairs of cycling shorts to women over the past three years to prevent upskirting.
body:
For three years, Elisabeth Polaczy has been quietly protecting visitors to one of Munich's most notorious attractions. The 80-year-old operator of the Teufelsrad, the Oktoberfest's spinning platform ride where skirts often fly up, has handed out more than 100 pairs of free cycling shorts during this year's festival alone. Her goal is simple: to shield women and girls from the thousands of people filming under their dresses for social media. "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure," Polaczy told the BBC. The measure emerged as a response to a disturbing problem. Investigators found that at least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have circulated online, some viewed millions of times. One woman reportedly earned €9,000 from a single clip. Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, carrying a potential two-year prison sentence, yet enforcement remains difficult when smartphones are ubiquitous in crowds.

Polaczy's initiative reflects a deeper shift at the festival. Some waitresses now wear cycling shorts beneath their traditional dirndls. Munich's city government has tightened regulations, banning live-streamed content and requiring filming permits. Police have increased arrests—including a 45-year-old Swiss man this year—and launched awareness campaigns warning against upskirting. Yet advocates argue the current law has gaps. Josephine Ballon, who heads the German non-profit Hate Aid, points out that existing legislation only applies when someone deliberately films under a skirt, not when a skirt naturally flies up and gets photographed. She calls for stronger protections and accountability for platforms hosting such content.

While systemic change moves slowly through courts and legislatures, Polaczy's quiet generosity offers something immediate: dignity and safety for festival-goers. Though donating hundreds of shorts costs her dearly, she considers it worthwhile.
quick_facts: Elisabeth Polaczy, 80, distributes free cycling shorts at Munich's Oktoberfest
Over 100 pairs handed out during the 2025 festival
At least 32,000 upskirting videos of Teufelsrad riders found in circulation
Upskirting carries up to two years in jail under German law
Police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for filming under a woman's dirndl
